blocks.text: Male reproductive system and microscopic anatomy of the testis

Human reproduction is sexual, viviparous (the young develop inside the mother) and involves internal fertilisation. The male system consists of a pair of **testes**, accessory ducts, accessory glands and the external genitalia. The testes lie outside the abdominal cavity in a pouch of skin called the **scrotum**. This position keeps the temperature of the testes 2 to 2.5 degrees Celsius lower than normal body temperature, which is necessary for the production of sperm.

Each testis is oval and is divided into about 250 compartments called **testicular lobules**. Every lobule contains one to three highly coiled **seminiferous tubules**, in which sperm are produced. The wall of a seminiferous tubule is lined on the inside by two types of cells: the **male germ cells** (spermatogonia), which undergo meiosis to form sperm, and the **Sertoli cells**, which provide nutrition to the developing germ cells. The spaces between the tubules, the interstitial spaces, contain small blood vessels and **interstitial cells (Leydig cells)**, which synthesise and secrete male hormones called **androgens** (mainly testosterone).
Large supporting cells in the wall of the seminiferous tubule. They nourish and support the developing germ cells and are stimulated by follicle stimulating hormone (FSH).

The seminiferous tubules open into the **vasa efferentia**, which leave the testis and open into the **epididymis** located along the posterior surface of each testis. The epididymis leads to the **vas deferens**, which ascends to the abdomen, loops over the urinary bladder and receives a duct from the **seminal vesicle** to form the **ejaculatory duct**. The ejaculatory ducts store and transport sperm and open into the **urethra**, which extends through the penis and ends at the urethral opening, the urethral meatus. The penis is the external genitalia, and its enlarged end is the **glans penis**, covered by a loose fold of skin, the foreskin.

The **accessory glands** are the paired seminal vesicles, a prostate gland and paired bulbourethral glands. Their secretions form the **seminal plasma**, rich in fructose, calcium and some enzymes. The secretions of the bulbourethral glands help in lubrication of the penis. The sperm and seminal plasma together make up the semen.
Female reproductive system and microscopic anatomy of the ovary

The female system consists of a pair of **ovaries**, a pair of **oviducts (fallopian tubes)**, a **uterus**, a **cervix**, a **vagina** and external genitalia, together with a pair of mammary glands. The ovaries are the primary female sex organs. They produce the female gamete (ovum) and several steroid hormones (ovarian hormones). The ovaries are located one on each side of the lower abdomen, and each is about 2 to 4 cm in length, connected to the pelvic wall and uterus by ligaments.

Each ovary is covered by a thin epithelium that encloses the ovarian **stroma**, which is divided into two zones: a peripheral cortex and an inner medulla. The cortex contains **ovarian follicles** at different stages of development.

Each oviduct is about 10 to 12 cm long and extends from the periphery of each ovary to the uterus. The part closest to the ovary is a funnel-shaped **infundibulum**, whose edges have finger-like projections called **fimbriae**; they help to collect the ovum after ovulation. The infundibulum leads to the wider **ampulla** and then to the narrow **isthmus**, which joins the uterus. The wall of the **uterus** has three layers: the external thin **perimetrium**, the middle thick **myometrium** of smooth muscle, which shows strong contractions during delivery, and the inner glandular **endometrium**, which lines the uterine cavity and undergoes cyclical changes during the menstrual cycle. The narrow lower part of the uterus is the **cervix**; the cervical canal together with the vagina forms the **birth canal**.

The mammary glands are paired structures that contain glandular tissue and fat. Each gland has 15 to 20 mammary lobes containing clusters of cells called **alveoli**. The cells of the alveoli secrete milk, which is stored in the cavities (lumen) of the alveoli. The alveoli open into mammary tubules, and the tubules of each lobe join to form a **mammary duct**. Several mammary ducts join to form a wider **mammary ampulla**, which is connected to **lactiferous ducts** through which milk is sucked out.

The testis is kept 2 to 2.5 degrees Celsius below body temperature in the scrotum. The wall of the seminiferous tubule contains Sertoli cells and spermatogonia, and the Leydig cells lie outside the tubules in the interstitial spaces and produce androgens.
Gametogenesis: spermatogenesis and oogenesis

**Gametogenesis** is the formation of gametes. In males it is **spermatogenesis** and in females **oogenesis**. In spermatogenesis, the **spermatogonia** (2n = 46) present on the inside wall of the seminiferous tubules multiply by mitotic division and increase in number. Each spermatogonium is diploid and contains 46 chromosomes. Some of the spermatogonia called **primary spermatocytes** periodically undergo meiosis. A primary spermatocyte completes the first meiotic division (reductional division) leading to formation of two equal haploid cells called **secondary spermatocytes**, which have only 23 chromosomes each. The secondary spermatocytes undergo the second meiotic division to produce four equal haploid **spermatids**. The spermatids are transformed into **spermatozoa (sperms)** by the process called **spermiogenesis**. After spermiogenesis, sperm heads become embedded in the Sertoli cells and are finally released from the seminiferous tubules by the process called **spermiation**.
One primary spermatocyte gives four functional sperm, each with 23 chromosomes in humans.

The hormone **GnRH** (gonadotropin releasing hormone) from the hypothalamus increases at puberty and acts on the anterior pituitary to release two gonadotropins: **LH** and **FSH**. LH acts on the Leydig cells and stimulates synthesis and secretion of androgens, which in turn stimulate the process of spermatogenesis. FSH acts on the Sertoli cells and stimulates secretion of some factors that help in the spermiogenesis. A mature sperm has a **head**, a **neck**, a **middle piece** and a **tail**. The head contains an elongated haploid nucleus, whose anterior portion is covered by a cap-like structure, the **acrosome**, filled with enzymes that help fertilisation of the ovum. The middle piece has numerous mitochondria, which produce energy for the movement of the tail that facilitates sperm motility essential for fertilisation. The human male ejaculates about 200 to 300 million sperms during a coitus, and for normal fertility at least 60 per cent of them must have normal shape and size and at least 40 per cent must show vigorous motility.

**Oogenesis** is the process of formation of a mature female gamete. It is initiated during the embryonic development stage, when millions of **oogonia** are formed within each foetal ovary; no more oogonia are formed or added after birth. These cells start division and enter prophase I of meiosis, and get temporarily arrested at that stage; they are then called **primary oocytes**. Each primary oocyte gets surrounded by a layer of granulosa cells and is called the **primary follicle**. A large number of follicles degenerate during the phase from birth to puberty, and at puberty only about 60,000 to 80,000 primary follicles are left in each ovary. The primary follicles get surrounded by more layers of granulosa cells and a new theca and are called **secondary follicles**. The secondary follicle soon transforms into a **tertiary follicle**, which is characterised by a fluid-filled cavity called the **antrum**. The primary oocyte within the tertiary follicle grows in size and completes its first meiotic division. It is an unequal division resulting in the formation of a large haploid **secondary oocyte** and a tiny **first polar body**. The tertiary follicle further changes into the mature follicle or **Graafian follicle**. The secondary oocyte is surrounded by a new membrane called the **zona pellucida**. The Graafian follicle now ruptures to release the secondary oocyte (ovum) from the ovary by the process called **ovulation**.

blocks.problem: An experimenter looks at 100 primary spermatocytes and 100 primary oocytes. How many functional sperm and how many functional ova can they produce, and what is the least number of polar bodies formed if all the ova are fertilised? Give the chromosome number of each cell type in a human.
blocks.solution: Each primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis I and II to give four haploid spermatids, which all become sperm, so 100 primary spermatocytes give $100 \times 4 = 400$ sperm. Each primary oocyte gives only one functional ovum, because the cytoplasm is divided unequally and the other cells are tiny polar bodies. Thus 100 primary oocytes give 100 ova. Each oocyte forms a first polar body at meiosis I and, if the ovum is fertilised, a second polar body at meiosis II (the first polar body may also divide), so there are at least 200 polar bodies. A primary spermatocyte and primary oocyte each have 46 chromosomes, and the sperm and ovum each have 23.
blocks.answer: 400 sperm; 100 ova and at least 200 polar bodies; 46 chromosomes in primary spermatocytes and oocytes, 23 in gametes

blocks.text: Menstrual cycle

The reproductive cycle in the female primates (monkeys, apes and human beings) is called the **menstrual cycle**. The first menstruation begins at puberty and is called **menarche**. In human females, menstruation is repeated at an average interval of about 28 to 29 days, and the cycle of events starting from one menstruation till the next is called the menstrual cycle. One ovum is released (ovulation) during the middle of each cycle. The cycle stops at about 50 years of age, which is called **menopause**. Cyclic menstruation is an indicator of normal reproductive phase and extends between menarche and menopause.

blocks.caption: Phases of a 28-day menstrual cycle
rows: Menstrual flow due to breakdown of the endometrial lining and its blood vessels; occurs when the ovum is not fertilised
Primary follicles grow into a Graafian follicle; the endometrium regenerates; FSH and oestrogen rise
Both LH and FSH reach a peak in the middle of the cycle (about day 14); the LH surge induces rupture of the Graafian follicle and release of the ovum
The remaining follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes large amounts of progesterone essential for the maintenance of the endometrium

blocks.text: If fertilisation does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates. This causes disintegration of the endometrium, leading to menstruation and a new cycle. In the absence of fertilisation the lack of progesterone leads to the shedding of the endometrial lining. If the ovum is fertilised, the corpus luteum continues to function and the cycle stops during pregnancy, so there are no menstrual cycles during pregnancy.

blocks.problem: In a woman with a regular 28-day cycle, day 1 is the first day of menstruation and ovulation occurs on day 14. On which day would the corpus luteum start to form, and how many days does the luteal phase last if it ends on day 28? If fertilisation occurs, which cells later produce hCG?
blocks.solution: Ovulation on day 14 releases the secondary oocyte and the follicle wall that remains in the ovary is converted into the corpus luteum, so it starts forming just after day 14, about day 15. It remains active from day 15 to day 28, which is $28 - 15 + 1 = 14$ days. During these 14 days it secretes progesterone that maintains the endometrium. If fertilisation occurs, the trophoblast cells of the blastocyst and later the placenta produce human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which maintains the corpus luteum so that progesterone secretion continues.
blocks.answer: Corpus luteum forms about day 15; luteal phase lasts 14 days; hCG comes from the trophoblast and placenta

blocks.text: Fertilisation, embryo development up to blastocyst and implantation

During copulation (coitus), semen is released by the penis into the vagina (**insemination**). The motile sperms swim rapidly, pass through the cervix, enter the uterus and finally reach the junction of the isthmus and the ampulla (ampullary-isthmic junction) of the fallopian tube. The ovum released by the ovary is also transported to the ampullary region, where **fertilisation** takes place. Fertilisation can only occur if the ovum and sperms are transported simultaneously to the ampullary-isthmic junction, which is why not all copulations lead to fertilisation and pregnancy.

During fertilisation, a sperm comes in contact with the zona pellucida layer of the ovum and induces changes in the membrane that block the entry of additional sperms. This ensures that only one sperm can fertilise an ovum. The secretions of the acrosome help the sperm enter the cytoplasm of the ovum through the zona pellucida and the plasma membrane. This induces the completion of the meiotic division of the secondary oocyte. The second meiotic division is also unequal and results in the formation of a second polar body and a haploid ovum (ootid). Soon the haploid nucleus of the sperm and that of the ovum fuse together to form a diploid **zygote**.

The zygote starts dividing as it moves through the isthmus of the oviduct towards the uterus. This process is called **cleavage**, and the mitotic divisions form 2, 4, 8 and 16 daughter cells called **blastomeres**. The embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres is called a **morula**. The morula continues to divide and transforms into a **blastocyst** as it moves further into the uterus. The blastomeres in the blastocyst are arranged into an outer layer called the **trophoblast** and an inner group of cells attached to it called the **inner cell mass**. The trophoblast layer then gets attached to the endometrium and the inner cell mass gets differentiated as the embryo. After attachment, the uterine cells divide rapidly and cover the blastocyst. As a result, the blastocyst becomes embedded in the endometrium of the uterus. This is called **implantation**, and it leads to pregnancy.

Fertilisation occurs in the ampullary-isthmic junction of the oviduct. The cleavage sequence is zygote, 2-cell, 4-cell, 8-cell, morula, blastocyst. The trophoblast attaches the blastocyst to the endometrium (implantation), and the inner cell mass becomes the embryo.
Pregnancy, embryonic development and the placenta

After implantation, finger-like projections called **chorionic villi** appear on the trophoblast and are surrounded by the uterine tissue and maternal blood. The chorionic villi and uterine tissue become interdigitated with each other and jointly form a structural and functional unit between the developing embryo (foetus) and the maternal body called the **placenta**. The placenta facilitates the supply of oxygen and nutrients to the embryo, and the removal of carbon dioxide and excretory wastes produced by the embryo. The placenta is connected to the embryo through an umbilical cord, which helps in the transport of substances to and from the embryo. The placenta also acts as an endocrine tissue and produces several hormones such as **human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)**, **human placental lactogen (hPL)**, oestrogens, progesterone and, in the later phase of pregnancy, relaxin. hCG, hPL and relaxin are produced in women only during pregnancy.

The inner cell mass contains certain cells called stem cells, which have the potency to give rise to all the tissues and organs. As the implantation proceeds, the inner cell mass differentiates into an outer layer called the **ectoderm** and an inner layer called the **endoderm**, and a **mesoderm** soon appears between them. These three germ layers give rise to all tissues of the adult. The human pregnancy lasts about nine months. The embryo's heart is formed after one month of pregnancy, and the first sign of growth of the foetus may be the heart sound heard by a doctor. By the end of the second month of pregnancy the foetus develops limbs and digits. By the end of the first trimester (12 weeks) most of the major organ systems are formed, for example the limbs and external genital organs are well developed. The first movements of the foetus and appearance of hair on the head are usually observed during the fifth month. By the end of about 24 weeks (the end of the second trimester) the body is covered with fine hair, the eye-lids separate and eyelashes are formed. By the end of nine months of pregnancy the foetus is fully developed and ready for delivery.
Parturition and lactation

The average duration of human pregnancy is about nine months, which is called the **gestation period**. Vigorous contraction of the uterus at the end of pregnancy causes expulsion or delivery of the foetus. This process of delivery of the foetus (childbirth) is called **parturition**. Parturition is induced by a complex neuroendocrine mechanism. The signals for parturition originate from the fully developed foetus and the placenta, which induce mild uterine contractions called the **foetal ejection reflex**. This triggers release of **oxytocin** from the maternal pituitary. Oxytocin acts on the uterine muscle and causes stronger uterine contractions, which in turn stimulate further secretion of oxytocin. The stimulatory reflex between the uterine contraction and oxytocin secretion continues resulting in stronger and stronger contractions. This leads to expulsion of the baby out of the uterus through the birth canal, which is the parturition. Soon after the infant is delivered, the placenta is also expelled out of the uterus.

The mammary glands of the female undergo differentiation during pregnancy and starts producing milk towards the end of pregnancy by the process called **lactation**. This helps the mother to feed the new-born. The milk produced during the initial few days of lactation is called **colostrum**, which contains several antibodies absolutely essential to develop resistance for the new-born baby. Breast-feeding during the initial period of infant growth is recommended by doctors for the development of a healthy baby. Lactation is controlled by the hormone **prolactin**, and the milk is ejected by the hormone oxytocin when the baby suckles.

Exam tips: learn the order of structures in the male duct system (seminiferous tubules, rete testis, vasa efferentia, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra). Remember who acts on which cell: LH on Leydig cells, FSH on Sertoli cells. One primary oocyte gives only one ovum, while one primary spermatocyte gives four sperm. Fertilisation is in the ampulla and implantation in the uterus. Common mistake: stating that the corpus luteum secretes oestrogen only; its main product is progesterone. Another is confusing the secondary oocyte (released at ovulation) with the mature ovum (formed only after the sperm enters).

questions.stem: Which cells of the testis secrete androgens?
questions.explanation: Leydig (interstitial) cells lie in the spaces between the seminiferous tubules and secrete androgens such as testosterone under the influence of LH. Sertoli cells, in contrast, nourish the germ cells, and granulosa cells belong to the ovary.

optionRationale.1: Sertoli cells provide nutrition to developing germ cells.
optionRationale.3: Spermatogonia are germ cells that divide to form sperm.
optionRationale.4: Granulosa cells surround the oocyte in the ovary.

questions.stem: The testes are located in the scrotum because sperm production requires a temperature that is
options: 10 degrees Celsius lower than body temperature
2 to 2.5 degrees Celsius higher than body temperature
2 to 2.5 degrees Celsius lower than body temperature
questions.explanation: The scrotum keeps the testes slightly cooler than the rest of the body, by about 2 to 2.5 degrees Celsius, which is the optimum for spermatogenesis. Higher temperature would impair sperm production.

optionRationale.1: Body temperature is too high for sperm production.
optionRationale.2: The difference is only about 2 to 2.5 degrees.
optionRationale.3: A higher temperature would harm sperm formation.

questions.objective: State why the testes lie in the scrotum

questions.stem: Fertilisation in humans normally takes place in the
options: Ampullary-isthmic junction of the fallopian tube
questions.explanation: The sperm and the ovum meet at the junction of the ampulla and the isthmus of the oviduct, where fertilisation occurs. The zygote then travels towards the uterus while dividing, and the blastocyst implants in the endometrium.

optionRationale.1: Implantation, not fertilisation, occurs in the uterus.
optionRationale.2: The vagina only receives the semen.
optionRationale.4: The cervix is the narrow lower part of the uterus.

questions.stem: Match the structure in List-I with its function in List-II.
questions.explanation: Sertoli cells nourish germ cells, Leydig cells secrete androgens, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, and the acrosome has enzymes that help sperm penetrate the ovum. This gives A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV.

optionRationale.2: This pairs Sertoli cells with progesterone secretion, which is wrong.
optionRationale.3: This pairs Sertoli cells with androgen secretion, which is the job of Leydig cells.
optionRationale.4: This pairs Sertoli cells with enzymes for penetration, which belongs to the acrosome.

questions.objective: Match reproductive structures with their functions

right: IV. Enzymes for penetrating the ovum

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly shows the order of stages in spermatogenesis?
options: Spermatogonia, secondary spermatocyte, primary spermatocyte, spermatid
Primary spermatocyte, spermatogonia, spermatid, secondary spermatocyte
Spermatid, spermatogonia, primary spermatocyte, secondary spermatocyte
Spermatogonia, primary spermatocyte, secondary spermatocyte, spermatid
questions.explanation: Spermatogonia (2n) multiply by mitosis, some become primary spermatocytes (2n), which complete meiosis I to form secondary spermatocytes (n), and meiosis II forms spermatids (n) that mature into sperm by spermiogenesis.

optionRationale.1: The primary spermatocyte comes before the secondary spermatocyte.

questions.stem: How many sperm and how many functional ova can be formed from 50 primary spermatocytes and 50 primary oocytes respectively?
questions.explanation: Each primary spermatocyte gives four sperm, so 50 give $50 \times 4 = 200$ sperm. Each primary oocyte gives only one functional ovum and polar bodies, so 50 give 50 ova.

optionRationale.1: A spermatocyte gives four sperm, not two.
optionRationale.2: This ignores that each spermatocyte gives four sperm.
optionRationale.4: Each oocyte gives only one ovum.

questions.stem: Assertion (A): The first meiotic division of the primary oocyte is unequal. Reason (R): It gives a large secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body so that the ovum retains most of the cytoplasm and food reserves.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The unequal division of the cytoplasm allows the secondary oocyte to keep nutrients required to support early embryonic development, while the polar body, which is small, degenerates. Hence both statements are true and R explains A.

optionRationale.2: R is the explanation of A.
optionRationale.4: A is true and R is also true.

questions.objective: Explain why oogenesis involves unequal division

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the menstrual cycle.
A. Ovulation occurs about the 14th day of a 28-day cycle.
B. The corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone.
C. Menstruation is caused by a rise in progesterone.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Ovulation happens at mid-cycle, after the LH surge, and the corpus luteum secretes progesterone that maintains the endometrium. Menstruation is caused by a fall in progesterone when the corpus luteum degenerates, so C is incorrect.

optionRationale.2: C is wrong, since a fall in progesterone causes menstruation.
optionRationale.3: C is wrong, and B is correct.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements about the menstrual cycle

questions.stem: Which hormone surge induces the rupture of the Graafian follicle and the release of the ovum?
questions.explanation: A surge of LH, together with FSH, reaches its peak in the middle of the cycle and induces rupture of the Graafian follicle, releasing the secondary oocyte. Progesterone is the main hormone of the luteal phase.

optionRationale.1: Progesterone is secreted after ovulation by the corpus luteum.
optionRationale.2: Oxytocin acts on the uterus during childbirth.

questions.stem: The structure formed from the outer layer of cells of the blastocyst, which attaches to the endometrium, is the
questions.explanation: The outer layer of the blastocyst is the trophoblast. It attaches to the endometrium during implantation and later gives rise to the chorionic villi of the placenta. The inner cell mass becomes the embryo.

optionRationale.1: The inner cell mass becomes the embryo proper.
optionRationale.2: The morula is a solid ball of 8 to 16 blastomeres.
optionRationale.4: The zona pellucida is the membrane around the ovum.

questions.objective: Identify the role of the trophoblast

questions.stem: A woman with a regular 28-day cycle has day 1 as the first day of menstruation. The cells lining her uterus are thickest and most secretory around day 24. The hormone mainly responsible for this is
questions.explanation: Days 15 to 28 form the luteal phase when the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which keeps the endometrium thick and glandular for possible implantation. hCG is produced only if an embryo implants, and she is not stated to be pregnant.

optionRationale.1: FSH is highest in the follicular phase and triggers follicle growth.
optionRationale.3: Oxytocin works at parturition and milk ejection.
optionRationale.4: hCG is produced only during pregnancy.

questions.objective: Apply hormone knowledge to the luteal phase

questions.stem: Assertion (A): Menstrual cycles stop during pregnancy. Reason (R): hCG from the trophoblast maintains the corpus luteum, so progesterone secretion continues and the endometrium is not shed.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: After implantation the trophoblast produces hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum functioning. Progesterone from it, and later from the placenta, maintains the endometrium, so there is no menstruation. Thus R correctly explains A.

optionRationale.2: R is the cause of A.
optionRationale.4: A is true and R is also true.

questions.objective: Explain the suppression of menstruation in pregnancy

questions.stem: Which of the following events happens last?
options: Fusion of the sperm and ovum nuclei
Completion of meiosis II in the secondary oocyte
questions.explanation: Sperm entry completes meiosis II, then the nuclei fuse to form the zygote, which cleaves to the morula and the blastocyst. The blastocyst finally embeds in the endometrium in implantation, which leads to pregnancy.

optionRationale.1: Syngamy happens early, right after sperm entry.
optionRationale.2: Meiosis II is completed on sperm entry, before syngamy.
optionRationale.3: The blastocyst forms before it can implant.

questions.objective: Sequence the events from fertilisation to implantation

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.
A. The placenta secretes hCG, hPL, oestrogens and progesterone.
B. Colostrum is rich in antibodies.
C. Oxytocin acts on the uterine muscle during parturition.
D. Prolactin causes ejection of the foetus.
Which are correct?
questions.explanation: The placenta is an endocrine tissue that secretes hCG, hPL, oestrogens and progesterone. Colostrum provides antibodies to the baby and oxytocin strengthens the uterine contractions at birth. Prolactin controls milk production and not ejection of the foetus, so D is wrong.

optionRationale.2: D is incorrect, and A is correct.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on the placenta and lactation

questions.stem: A primary oocyte of a human foetus is arrested at which stage, and when is meiosis II finally completed?
questions.explanation: Primary oocytes begin meiosis in the foetus and are arrested in prophase I until puberty. Meiosis I is completed before ovulation, and the secondary oocyte is arrested at metaphase II, completing meiosis II only when a sperm enters at fertilisation.

optionRationale.1: The arrest is in prophase I, and meiosis II is not completed at birth.
optionRationale.3: Meiosis II is not completed at ovulation but on sperm entry.
optionRationale.4: The primary oocyte is not at anaphase II.
